legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 14 pages (45,537 chars) read, including appendices A (task list) and B (Table 3 full BABILong). No extraction faults, no embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "LM2: Large Memory Models". Jikun Kang, Wenqi Wu, Filippos Christianos, Alex J. Chan, Fraser Greenlee, George Thomas, Marvin Purtorab, Andy Toulis. All at Convergence Labs Ltd. Preprint, arXiv:2502.06049v1 [cs.CL], 9 Feb 2025. No peer-reviewed venue stated.

MAIN CLAIM: A decoder-only Llama-3-style Transformer gets a separate memory bank inside every decoder block. Tokens read it by cross attention. Input, forget and output gates update it. The memory path runs beside the normal attention path (skip connection), so the model keeps its general ability while gaining long-context multi-hop reasoning. The memory is in the weights/hidden states (a learned module), not in an external store or the prompt.

MECHANISM (p.3-4): memory bank M with N slots, each d wide. Input embeddings are queries, memory is keys and values. Output gate: E_next = E_attn + g_out·M. Update: M_{t+1} = g_in·tanh(E_mem) + g_forget·M_t. Config (p.4): 16 decoder blocks, d=2048, 2,048 memory slots, memory in all 16 blocks. About 1.2B base params plus 0.5B memory params = 1.7B total.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. BABILong, 0K (bAbI, no haystack), quote p.6: "LM2-1.7B achieves the highest average accuracy of 92.5%, surpassing Llama-3.2-1.2B, vanilla-LLama-1.7B, and RMT-1.7B, which average results are 40.7%, 75.0% and 76.4%". Setup: 10 tasks, 100 items per task (inferred from whole-number scores; the paper does not state a sample size). Baselines: vanilla-Llama-1.7B pretrained on the same data; RMT-1.7B on the same backbone, fine-tuned on bAbI; Llama-3.2-1.2B is Meta's model.
2. BABILong at 4K (p.6): LM2 55.9 vs vanilla 42.2, Llama-3.2-1.2B 36.8, RMT 38.4 (Table 1). The text says RMT is 48.4, which contradicts the table's 38.4. Table 1 is the version to trust.
3. BABILong, 8K to 128K aggregate (Table 1): LM2 39.9, RMT 35.5, Llama-3.2-1.2B-RAG 32.3, vanilla 31.2, Llama-3.2-1.2B 28.2. The gap narrows a lot at length. Most of LM2's long-context advantage comes from qa7 (counting): 92.8 against RMT's 73.3. On qa1 it scores 23.8 against 17.5 for RMT. RAG beats LM2 on qa4 and qa5 (e.g. qa5 72.0 vs 38.8).
4. MMLU (p.7, Table 2): average 29.4 for LM2, 28.0 for vanilla-Llama, 26.5 for RMT. These sit barely above the 25% chance level for 4-choice questions, so the "5.0% improvement" in the abstract is relative, not absolute (about +1.4 points).
The abstract's "37.1% over RMT, 86.3% over Llama-3.2" are relative averages across lengths. I did not re-derive them.

QUOTES
- p.1 (abstract): "LM2 model outperforms both the memory-augmented RMT model by 37.1% and the baseline Llama-3.2 model by 86.3% on average across tasks."
- p.7: "LM2 demonstrates a clear performance gain, improving the average accuracy of vanilla-Llama from 28.0% to 29.4%. On the contrary, ... RMT degrades the performance of vanilla-Llama to 26.5%."

ABLATION (p.7-8, Fig 5): memory in only the first block performs about like vanilla but converges more slowly. Memory in 6, 12 and 16 blocks gives lower perplexity, and 16 is best. This was trained on up to about 175B tokens, from the figure axis.

PRETRAINING (p.5): SmolLM-Corpus with Python removed, 28B tokens of synthetic textbooks and stories plus 220B tokens of FineWeb-Edu.

LIMITS / NOT SHOWN
- Only one size (1.7B), no scaling study, one run each, no error bars.
- Accuracy is far from good at long context. Several qa tasks fall to 12-24% at 8K or more, and the gains at length are small except for counting.
- The comparison is not like for like. RMT is fine-tuned on bAbI, while LM2 is pretrained with the memory. The Llama-3.2 baselines were trained on different data. Llama-3.2-1.2B has no 128K result in Table 3, and the RAG baseline is not described.
- MMLU scores are near chance, so the "no degradation" claim is weak evidence.
- Interpretability (4.4) and test-time adaptation (4.5) are single-example qualitative cases (one MMLU question, slots 1679, 1684 and 1). The slot "explanations" come from an LLM-based Neuron Explainer. The paper gives no quantitative evidence of what the memory stores.
- No latency, compute or memory cost is reported, despite the claim of "computational efficiency". There is no comparison with other recent long-context methods (it dismisses ARMT and MemReasoner as weaker than RMT), and no test of agent or persistent cross-session memory.
- The text says "test-time updates" happen, but the memory is updated on each forward pass within one context. Nothing persists across sessions.
- There is no explicit limitations section.

BUILDS ON: Recurrent Memory Transformer (Bulatov et al., 2022); Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019); Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020); Big Bird (Zaheer et al., 2020); GMAT (Gupta & Berant, 2020); ETC (Ainslie et al., 2020); ARMT (Rodkin et al., 2024); MemReasoner (Ko et al., 2024, NeurIPS'24 System-2 Reasoning workshop); BABILong (Kuratov et al., 2024); bAbI (Weston et al., 2016, ICLR); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020); Llama 3 (Dubey et al., 2024); MMLU (Hendrycks et al., ICLR 2021); Neuron Explainer (Bills et al., 2023); SmolLM-Corpus (2023).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1, p.2 (architecture). It shows the gray normal attention flow, the pink memory flow, and the input, output and forget gates around the memory bank, and it explains the design faster than the text does. Alternatives are Fig 2 (the three gating phases inside one block, p.4) and Fig 5 (perplexity against the number of memory blocks, p.8). I did not run the figure caption script.
